title: How an Octopus Can Squeeze into a Beer Can - Nautilus
gist: Teaser on a Journal of Experimental Biology study by Wenci Xin (National University of Singapore) and coauthors on how octopuses compress their bodies to pass through small holes. It tested Octopus vulgaris and Octopus maya with holes sized relative to eye distance; the subtitle suggests the ability varies by species.

themes.theme: Octopus body compression and soft-robotics relevance

insights.claim: A study in the Journal of Experimental Biology, led by mechanical engineer Wenci Xin of the National University of Singapore with coauthors from Italy and Austria, examined how octopuses compress their bodies to squeeze through small spaces as refuge behavior.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Because a mechanical engineer led the study, it likely points to soft-robotics applications of octopus compression mechanics.

insights.claim: The experiments used three subadult common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) collected by fishermen in France and four juvenile Mexican four-eyed octopuses (Octopus maya) raised from eggs in the lab.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: The sample is very small (seven animals), so treat the findings as preliminary.

insights.claim: Each octopus had to pass through a barrier hole that was large or small relative to its eye distance; eye spacing served as a proxy for head capsule size.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Standardizing hole size to body size is a reusable way to benchmark compressibility.
insights.quote: Octopus eyes sit on either side of their head capsule and thus prove a good proxy for head capsule size

insights.claim: The article suggests the ability to squeeze into tight spaces differs between octopus species, though the excerpt cuts off before the results.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Differences between species could reveal which body mechanics enable extreme compression.
insights.quote: Or not, depending on the species
